title: Raman-detected quantum dot microscopy for nanoscale electrostatic potential imaging
authors: Jiří Doležal, Amandeep Sagwal, Rodrigo Cezar de Campos Ferreira, Martin Švec
abstract: Quantification of electrostatic potentials at the nanoscale is crucial for understanding the principles governing properties of materials across multiple length scales. Currently, one of the most successful approaches relies on the charging response of a molecular quantum dot, suspended on a tip of a scanning probe microscope and measured using dynamic force spectroscopy. We investigate the possibility of an optical detection, aiming to improve the speed and reduce the complexity of this measurement scheme. We show that the integrated tip-enhanced Raman scattering intensity strongly correlates with the charge state of the quantum dot, and use it to map the electrostatic potential of a single atom. A quantitative equivalence with the established force spectroscopy method is found. We address the underlying photophysical principle of this new method by measuring the Raman spectra as a function of excitation wavelength and the molecular quantum dot charge. We reveal that the observed Raman intensity variations are primarily driven by transitions between resonant and non-resonant Raman scattering regimes of the molecule.
summary: The research introduces an advanced technique using Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) to map electrostatic potentials on surfaces. By monitoring changes in the molecule's Raman signal as it charges, researchers can achieve quantitative measurements equivalent to traditional force microscopy methods. This offers a powerful, optically driven tool for understanding charge dynamics at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an optical detection method for quantifying electrostatic potentials at the nanoscale, overcoming limitations in speed and complexity associated with traditional force spectroscopy techniques.
main_result: The integrated Tip-Enhanced Raman Scattering (TERS) intensity was shown to correlate strongly with the quantum dot's charge state, allowing for quantitative mapping of the electrostatic potential ($\Phi_S$) with accuracy comparable to established AFM methods.
method: Electrostatic potential is mapped by measuring the charging threshold voltages ($V_+$ and $V_-$) using a feedback loop controlling the TERS signal intensity. This technique replaces force measurements ($\Delta f(V)$) with optical detection of molecular charge state changes.
model_or_system: The experiment uses molecular quantum dots (PTCDA molecules) suspended on an atomically sharp tip, measured via Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) in a Scanning Probe Microscopy setup. The potential mapping relies on the charging response of these QDs.
key_observables: Integrated TERS intensity ($I_{APD}(V)$), charge state switching thresholds ($V_+$, $V_-$), and the reconstructed electrostatic potential map ($\Phi_S(x, y)$).
important_parameters: Bias voltage ($V$), excitation wavelength (e.g., 1.58 eV, 1.96 eV, 2.33 eV), and tip-sample geometry parameters.
main_assumptions: The reconstruction of the potential assumes a sphere-on-sphere tip geometry model; systematic errors like upward shifts in $V_-$ due to illumination are noted but deemed negligible for dipole moment quantification.
figures_summary: Figures compare TERS intensity vs. force shift ($\Delta f(V)$) responses, show direct mapping of $\Phi_S$ around adatoms on Ag(111), and illustrate the bias-dependent spectral changes (Stark shifts) in TERS spectra.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for nanoscale potential measurement to demonstrating the TERS detection method. It compares this optical approach against established force spectroscopy, details the quantitative mapping process using feedback control, and finally analyzes the underlying photophysical mechanism driving the signal variation.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics (Raman scattering) with surface science/condensed matter physics by providing a non-contact, optically enhanced method to probe local electronic structure and potential landscapes at the atomic scale.
